diseases.name: Apple Scab

diseases.causes: Cool, wet spring weather; the fungus overwinters in fallen leaves.
diseases.effect: Infected leaves drop early; fruit is blemished and cracks.

conditions: Leaves staying wet for several hours.
Fallen leaves left under the tree.
A crowded canopy that dries slowly.

steps.title: Rake up fallen leaves
steps.instruction: Collect and destroy fallen leaves under the tree.
steps.rationale: Next spring's spores come from last year's leaves.

steps.title: Prune for airflow
steps.instruction: Thin crowded branches so the canopy dries quickly.

Leaves yellow and drop from the bottom up.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off spotted lower leaves and bag them.
steps.rationale: Removes the spores that splash up to healthy leaves.

steps.title: Mulch and water at the base
steps.instruction: Mulch the soil and water at the base, not over the leaves.
steps.rationale: Mulch stops spores splashing up from the soil.

steps.title: Apply a protectant fungicide
steps.instruction: Spray a registered product, following the label.
steps.rationale: Protects new leaves from infection.

prevention.title: Clear tomato debris after harvest
prevention.detail: The fungus survives on old plant remains.

prevention.title: Rotate for at least a year

diseases.name: Spider Mites
diseases.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae): tiny sap-sucking mites, not a disease.
diseases.causes: Hot, dry weather and dusty, water-stressed plants; mites multiply very fast in heat.
diseases.effect: Feeding empties leaf cells; leaves bronze, dry out and drop.
diseases.untreated: Heavy infestations can strip and kill plants in hot weather.
symptoms: Fine pale stippling (tiny dots) on the leaves
Leaves turn yellow-bronze and dry
Fine webbing under leaves and at the tips
lifecycle: Mites overwinter on weeds and sheltered plants.
In hot, dry weather they move onto crops.
They feed under the leaves, leaving pale dots.
Numbers explode in days; leaves bronze and webbing appears.

steps.title: Hose the mites off
steps.instruction: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water.
steps.rationale: Knocks mites and webbing off and raises the humidity they dislike.

steps.title: Remove the worst leaves
steps.instruction: Take off heavily webbed leaves and bag them.
steps.rationale: Removes many mites and eggs at once.

steps.title: Use a registered miticide or soap
steps.instruction: Apply insecticidal soap, oil or a registered miticide, following the label; spare predatory mites.
steps.rationale: Reduces the population while natural enemies recover.

prevention.title: Check leaf undersides in hot weather
prevention.detail: Look for stippling and webbing every few days.

prevention.title: Protect natural enemies
prevention.detail: Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill predatory mites.

methods.name: Conserve or release predatory mites
methods.purpose: Suppresses mites without harming natural enemies

methods.name: Correct water stress and dust
methods.limitations: Does not remove a colony alone.

methods.name: Directed water wash, then labelled insecticidal soap or oil

followups.finding: Few active mites; the new leaf is less damaged.
followups.escalation: If mites rebound, reassess the route and conditions.

followups.finding: Old stippling remains.

diseases.recoveryNote: Old stippling stays. Fewer active mites means the speckling stops spreading and later growth is cleaner.

diseases.name: Target Spot
diseases.description: A fungal disease (Corynespora cassiicola) of tomato leaves, stems and fruit.
diseases.causes: Warm, humid weather with long leaf wetness; dense canopies; spores survive on debris.
diseases.effect: Spots merge and leaves drop, starting in the lower canopy.
diseases.untreated: Defoliation and fruit spots reduce yield and quality.

Brown spots with concentric rings appear.
Spots merge and leaves drop.

steps.title: Remove spotted leaves

steps.rationale: Reduces the spores in the canopy.

steps.title: Open up the canopy
steps.instruction: Prune lower leaves and side shoots so air moves through.
steps.rationale: Leaves dry faster, so fewer spores infect.

steps.title: Apply a protectant fungicide
steps.instruction: Spray a registered product, following the label.
steps.rationale: Protects new growth.

prevention.title: Remove crop debris

prevention.title: Space and prune
prevention.detail: A dry, open canopy is the best defence.

methods.name: Effective fungicide programme with resistance management

diseases.name: Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
diseases.description: A virus (TYLCV, a begomovirus) spread by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
diseases.causes: Whiteflies that fed on infected plants carry the virus to healthy ones; warm weather favours them.
diseases.effect: Infected plants stop growing and set little or no fruit.
diseases.untreated: There is no cure: infected plants stay infected and are a source for the whiteflies.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and cup
Yellow leaf edges
Small, crumpled new leaves; stunted plants
Flowers drop, few fruit
lifecycle: Whiteflies pick up the virus from infected plants.
They carry it to healthy plants as they feed.
New leaves come out small, curled and yellow-edged.
The plant stops growing and sets little fruit.
conditions: No insect-proof cover on young plants.

steps.title: Remove infected plants
steps.instruction: Pull out clearly infected plants and bag them right away.
steps.rationale: They cannot be cured and they feed the whiteflies that spread the virus.

steps.title: Control the whiteflies
steps.instruction: Use yellow sticky traps and insect-proof mesh; treat whiteflies with a registered product if needed.
steps.rationale: Stopping the carrier is the only way to protect the remaining plants.

steps.title: Clear weeds and volunteers
steps.instruction: Remove weeds and self-sown tomatoes around the crop.
steps.rationale: They can hold both the virus and the whiteflies.

prevention.title: Plant resistant varieties
prevention.detail: TYLCV-resistant varieties are the most reliable protection.

prevention.title: Watch for whiteflies
prevention.detail: Check leaf undersides and sticky traps weekly.

methods.name: Contain vectors, then remove infected material
methods.purpose: Stops it acting as a virus source

followups.finding: Healthy replacement established; few whiteflies on the card.
followups.escalation: If counts rise, review exclusion.

diseases.recoveryNote: This leaf cannot be saved by treatment. Correct containment stops it acting as a source; recovery means replacing it with clean stock.

diseases.name: Bacterial Leaf Streak (Black Chaff)
diseases.description: A bacterial disease of wheat that streaks the leaves and blackens the glumes of the head.
diseases.causes: Bacteria come in on seed and spread by rain and wind in warm, wet weather.
diseases.effect: Leaf area and grain fill fall.
diseases.untreated: No chemical control works well.
symptoms: Narrow, water-soaked streaks between the leaf veins
Streaks turn brown; droplets of bacterial ooze dry into flakes
Dark purple-black streaks on the glumes (black chaff)
lifecycle: Bacteria come in on seed.
Rain and wind spread them.
Water-soaked streaks form between the veins.
Glumes blacken as the head forms.

steps.title: Confirm with the ooze
steps.instruction: Look for shiny dried ooze flakes on the streaks.
steps.rationale: Separates it from fungal streaks.

steps.title: Plan clean seed
steps.instruction: Use seed from healthy fields.
steps.rationale: Seed carries the bacteria.

steps.title: Rotate crops
steps.instruction: Leave a year away from wheat and barley.
steps.rationale: Residue carries it.

diseases.name: Wheat Blast
diseases.description: A fast, destructive disease of wheat heads, first seen in Brazil and since 2016 in Bangladesh and Zambia.
diseases.causes: Spores spread by wind and on seed; warm, wet weather at heading lets them infect the rachis and kill the head above it.
diseases.effect: Bleached heads give little or no grain.
diseases.untreated: Outbreaks can destroy whole fields within days.
symptoms: Heads bleached white above the infection point, while the lower part stays green
A dark, shiny lesion on the rachis where it was infected
Shrivelled or no grain in the bleached part
lifecycle: Spores come in on seed or wind.
Warm, wet weather at heading lets them infect.
A lesion on the rachis cuts off the head above it.
The head bleaches and sets little grain.

steps.title: Report suspected blast
steps.instruction: Tell the local extension service: it is a quarantine disease in many places.
steps.rationale: Early reports slow its spread.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at heading where advised on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Sprays only protect; they cannot save bleached heads.

steps.title: Do not save the seed
steps.instruction: Do not keep seed from affected fields.
steps.rationale: Seed carries the fungus to new areas.

prevention.title: Sow clean seed of resistant varieties
prevention.detail: Seed carries it; some varieties resist.

prevention.title: Sow early
prevention.detail: Avoids warm, wet weather at heading.

diseases.name: Fusarium Head Blight (Scab)
diseases.description: A fungal disease of wheat heads that bleaches spikelets and contaminates grain with mycotoxins.
diseases.causes: Spores from maize and wheat residue infect the heads at flowering in warm, wet weather.
diseases.effect: Yield falls and grain may contain mycotoxins (DON).
diseases.untreated: Contaminated grain can be rejected.
symptoms: Bleached spikelets on a still-green head
Pink-orange spore masses at the base of spikelets
Shrivelled, chalky 'tombstone' kernels
lifecycle: The fungus survives on maize and wheat residue.
Spores reach the heads at flowering.
Spikelets bleach; pink spores form.
Kernels shrivel and carry mycotoxins.

steps.title: Note how many heads are bleached
steps.instruction: Count affected heads.
steps.rationale: Guides harvest and grain testing.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at early flowering on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Only flowering-time sprays help.

steps.title: Test the grain
steps.instruction: Have harvested grain tested for mycotoxins.
steps.rationale: Contaminated grain is a health risk.

prevention.title: Do not follow maize with wheat

diseases.name: Leaf Blight (Spot Blotch)
diseases.description: The main leaf blight of wheat in warm, humid regions such as the plains of South Asia.
diseases.causes: The fungus comes in on seed and residue; spores spread by wind and rain in warm, humid weather after heading.
diseases.effect: Dried leaves cut grain fill; grain is shrivelled and black-pointed.
diseases.untreated: Severe in late-sown, warm crops.
symptoms: Small, dark brown, oval spots on the lower leaves
Spots grow into long brown blotches with yellow edges
Blotches join; leaves dry from the tip down
lifecycle: The fungus survives on seed and residue.
Spores reach the lower leaves.
Brown blotches grow and join.

steps.title: Scout the upper leaves
steps.instruction: Check the flag leaf and the leaf below for blotches.
steps.rationale: These leaves fill the grain.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at heading where advised on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

steps.title: Plan the next crop
steps.instruction: Sow on time, with clean seed of a tolerant variety.
steps.rationale: Late sowing meets the warm, humid weather it needs.

diseases.name: Leaf Rust (Brown Rust)
diseases.description: A rust fungus of wheat leaves with scattered orange-brown pustules.
diseases.causes: Spores blow long distances on the wind; dew on the leaves lets them infect, and new spores form within one to two weeks.
diseases.effect: Rusted leaves lose their green area, so grain fill suffers.
diseases.untreated: Severe epidemics can cut yield heavily.

diseases.name: Loose Smut
diseases.description: A seed-borne fungal disease that replaces the wheat head with a mass of black spores.
diseases.causes: The fungus lives inside the seed embryo; infected seed grows into plants whose heads are spore masses that infect neighbouring flowers.
diseases.effect: Infected heads produce no grain.
diseases.untreated: Spores infect neighbouring flowers, so next year's seed is infected.
symptoms: Heads emerge as masses of olive-black spores instead of grain
Spores blow away, leaving a bare stalk (rachis)
Infected heads emerge a little earlier and taller
lifecycle: The fungus waits inside the seed.

Heads emerge as black spore masses.
Spores infect neighbouring flowers' seed.

steps.title: Do not save seed from this field

steps.rationale: Reaches the fungus inside the seed.
